1812-09-25.summary: Barlow reports that indemnities for past spoliations are at last under discussion on a footing more favorable than he expected, that his note of June has convinced everyone in the imperial confidence, that the Emperor's decision is expected in a few days, and that the treaty will meet no difficulty once the mode of indemnity is agreed.
1812-09-25.en:
A short letter in a secretary's hand, signed by Barlow, the American minister in Paris, to the Secretary of State.
It acknowledges Monroe's letters and reports on the negotiation with France. Only the middle paragraph is in code:
there Barlow says that indemnities for past spoliations (the American claims for ships and cargoes seized by
France) are at last under discussion, that the men about the Emperor have been won over, and that the treaty will
follow once the form of the indemnity is settled. Barlow left Paris for Wilna a month later to conclude it and
died on the road back, on 26 December 1812; nothing was signed.

The whole letter is given. It is English, so there is no translation.

Barlow's clear text is plain. Words written in code are in italics.

1812-10-25.summary: Accepting Bassano's invitation to Wilna, Barlow warns that if the project (the treaty of commerce and the convention of indemnities), whose execution would cost the imperial treasury little or nothing, is rejected, the President can see in it nothing but a determined refusal of justice on the part of his Imperial Majesty, which must embarrass the American government in its operations in regard to England as well as France.
1812-10-25.en:
Barlow's last note to the French foreign minister before he set out for Wilna, where the Duke of Bassano had
invited him to finish the negotiation. He accepts, says the treaty of commerce and the convention of indemnities
are ready, and warns that the President will take a rejection as a refusal of justice. The note Bassano received
was presumably in clear. In the two copies sent home the sharpest words are in code: that the project would cost the imperial treasury little or nothing, and that the President could see in a rejection
nothing but a determined refusal of justice by the Emperor, which would embarrass the American government in its
dealings with England as well as France. Barlow died on the road back from Wilna on 26 December 1812.

The clear text is copy A, in full; copy B differs from it in about 24 small places (collationcopyB.md).

system: The numerical code of the United States legation in Paris, 1811-1813: words and syllables as numbers from 7 to 1700 (the = 1700, of = 631, and = 513, to = 494), written among clear words. Used by Barlow, by Monroe and Madison writing to him, and by Thomas…
